questions.answer_d: If the radio amateur can maintain the technical facilities personally

questions.question: What is required for a radio amateur to be allowed to operate an amateur station as a repeater or beacon?
questions.answer_a: A call sign assignment for operating a remotely controlled or automatically operating amateur station is required.
questions.answer_b: A licence of the highest amateur radio class is required.
questions.answer_c: Operating a repeater or beacon requires having held a valid amateur radio licence for at least 2 years.
questions.answer_d: No special conditions have to be met.

questions.question: Who may be given access to a club station in remote operation?
questions.answer_a: Only members of the group of radio amateurs that operates the club station
questions.answer_b: Only members of the group of radio amateurs entered in the assignment document
questions.answer_c: Only radio amateurs registered with the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) in writing or electronically
questions.answer_d: Only radio amateurs who cannot visit the club station in person

questions.question: Why must the operator of the "remote station" give contact details to the BNetzA?
questions.answer_a: The operator must be reachable by the BNetzA as a contact person.
questions.answer_b: The contact details are used for monthly invoicing for the "remote station".
questions.answer_c: The amateur radio societies' Intruder Watch uses the contact details for data matching, so as to identify the operator of the "remote station" in the event of interference.
questions.answer_d: The contact details for remote operation are listed in the BNetzA's call sign list.

questions.question: Who may transmit with an amateur station in "remote operation"? Radio amateurs authorised by the operator of the amateur station who ...
questions.answer_b: hold a Class A or E licence.
questions.answer_c: hold a Class A, E or N licence.
questions.answer_d: have held a licence for at least one year.

questions.question: What must be observed when the right to use a "remote station" is transferred to other radio amateurs?
questions.answer_a: The operator must ensure that only radio amateurs authorised by the operator can use the station.
questions.answer_b: Access to the use of the "remote station" must be open to all radio amateurs.
questions.answer_c: The users of the "remote station" may not carry out training operation.
questions.answer_d: The radio amateurs must hold at least a Class E amateur radio licence.

questions.question: How must the operator ensure the operational safety of the "remote station"? The operator must ensure that ...
questions.answer_a: the "remote station" is under the operator's indirect control.
questions.answer_b: no home-built components are used for the "remote station".
questions.answer_c: the "remote station" has an uninterruptible power supply.
questions.answer_d: a technical log of the use of the "remote station" is kept.

questions.question: Which of the following amateur stations may be used as a "remote station"?
questions.answer_c: Amateur stations with a Class N personal call sign
questions.answer_d: Amateur stations with a Class E personal call sign

questions.question: Who may operate a "remote station"?
questions.answer_b: Class A and E radio amateurs
questions.answer_c: Class A, E and N radio amateurs
questions.answer_d: Radio amateurs who have held a licence for at least one year

questions.question: Is an operating notification to the BNetzA required for "remote operation"?
questions.answer_a: Yes, for the operator of the remote station
questions.answer_b: Yes, for the user of the remote station
questions.answer_c: Yes, for the operator and the user of the remote station
questions.answer_d: No, there is no obligation to notify.

questions.question: What do radio amateurs mean by "remote operation"?
questions.answer_a: Operation in which a distant amateur station is operated, e.g. via the internet
questions.answer_b: Operation over very long distances (more than 500 km on VHF, more than 2000 km on HF)
questions.answer_c: Local control of a radio station by a computer standing next to it
questions.answer_d: Operation in contests by several radio amateurs who share out the tasks

sections.title: Frequency ranges and frequency usage parameters

questions.question: What is the maximum permitted effective radiated power (ERP) for radio amateurs with licence class N on the 10 m band?
In which of the following amateur frequency ranges is the maximum permitted occupied bandwidth of an emission 2 MHz, or 7 MHz for amplitude-modulated television transmissions?
In which of the following amateur frequency ranges is the maximum permitted occupied bandwidth of an emission 40 kHz?
In which of the following amateur frequency ranges is the maximum permitted occupied bandwidth of an emission 7 kHz?
In which of the following amateur frequency ranges is the maximum permitted occupied bandwidth of an emission 2.7 kHz?
In which amateur frequency ranges is the maximum permitted occupied bandwidth of an emission 800 Hz?
questions.answer_a: 135.7 to 137.8 kHz, 472 to 479 kHz and 10100 to 10150 kHz
questions.answer_b: 1810 to 2000 kHz, 3500 to 3800 kHz and 7000 to 7200 kHz

questions.question: What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power for Class E call sign holders on the amateur bands between 1300 MHz and 250 GHz?
What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power for Class A call sign holders on the amateur bands between 1300 MHz and 250 GHz?
What is the maximum permitted transmit power for Class A call sign holders in the frequency range 1240 to 1300 MHz?
questions.answer_a: 750 W PEP, but only a maximum of 5 W EIRP in the 1247 to 1263 MHz segment
questions.answer_d: 75 W PEP, but only a maximum of 5 W EIRP in the 1247 to 1263 MHz segment

questions.question: Which power limits apply to Class A and E call sign holders in the frequency ranges 144 to 146 MHz and 430 to 440 MHz?
questions.answer_a: A maximum of 750 W PEP for Class A and 75 W PEP for Class E
questions.answer_b: A maximum of 750 W PEP for both classes
questions.answer_c: A maximum of 100 W PEP for Class A and 50 W PEP for Class E
questions.answer_d: A maximum of 10 W PEP for both classes

questions.question: Which power limits apply to Class A and E call sign holders in the frequency ranges 21.000 to 21.450 MHz and 28.000 to 29.700 MHz?
questions.answer_a: A maximum of 750 W PEP for Class A and a maximum of 100 W PEP for Class E
questions.answer_b: A maximum of 200 W PEP for both classes
questions.answer_c: A maximum of 100 W PEP for Class A and a maximum of 10 W PEP for Class E
questions.answer_d: A maximum of 100 W PEP for both classes

questions.question: What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power for Class A call sign holders in the frequency ranges 21.000 to 21.450 MHz and 24.890 to 24.990 MHz?
What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power for Class A call sign holders in the frequency ranges 14.000 to 14.350 MHz and 18.068 to 18.168 MHz?
What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power for Class A call sign holders in the frequency range 10.1 to 10.15 MHz?
What applies to Class A and E call sign holders in the frequency range 3.5 to 3.8 MHz?
questions.answer_a: A maximum of 750 W PEP for Class A and a maximum of 100 W PEP for Class E
questions.answer_b: A maximum of 10 W PEP for both classes
questions.answer_c: A maximum of 750 W PEP for both classes
questions.answer_d: A maximum of 150 W PEP for Class A and a maximum of 10 W PEP for Class E

questions.question: What is the maximum permitted transmitter output power for Class A call sign holders in the frequency range 3.5 to 3.8 MHz?
What applies to Class E call sign holders in the frequency range 1810 to 1850 kHz?

You hold a Class N authorisation for the amateur service and use a radio with a transmitter output power of 5 W. When transmitting on the 2 m band, may you use a directly connected antenna with a gain of 1.8 (as a power ratio) relative to the isotropic radiator (equivalent to a gain of 2.6 dBi)?
questions.answer_a: Yes, because the radiated power does not exceed the limit of 10 W EIRP.
questions.answer_b: Yes, except when the amateur station is operated at a fixed location.
questions.answer_c: No, because the result is a radiated power of more than 10 W EIRP.
questions.answer_d: No, because I may not use antennas with gain.

questions.question: You hold a Class N authorisation for the amateur service and use a radio with a transmitter output power of 5 W. When transmitting on the 2 m band, may you use a directly connected antenna with a gain of 2.5 (as a power ratio) relative to the isotropic radiator (equivalent to a gain of 4.0 dBi)?
questions.answer_a: No, because the result is a radiated power of more than 10 W EIRP.
questions.answer_b: No, because I may not use antennas with gain.
questions.answer_c: Yes, because the transmitter output power does not exceed the limit of 10 W EIRP.
questions.answer_d: Yes, provided it is a handheld transceiver.

questions.question: What is the maximum permitted equivalent isotropically radiated power (EIRP) for radio amateurs with licence class N on the 2 m and 70 cm bands?
On which frequency ranges may radio amateurs with a Class N licence transmit?
questions.answer_a: 28 to 29.7 MHz, 144 to 146 MHz, 430 to 440 MHz
questions.answer_b: 7 to 7.2 MHz, 14 to 14.35 MHz, 1240 to 1300 MHz
questions.answer_c: On all HF frequency ranges allocated to amateur radio in Germany
questions.answer_d: On all frequency ranges above HF allocated to amateur radio in Germany

questions.question: Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 13 cm amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 23 cm amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 70 cm amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 2 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 6 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 10 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 12 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 15 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 17 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 20 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 30 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 40 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 80 m amateur band in Germany?
Which answer gives the correct lower and upper band edges of the 160 m amateur band in Germany?
What does the note that the frequency range 433.05 to 434.79 MHz is allocated as an ISM band mean?
questions.answer_a: This frequency range is also used for industrial, scientific, medical, domestic or similar applications.
questions.answer_b: This frequency range is used for international satellite measurements; this can cause interference to normal radio communication.
questions.answer_c: This frequency range is used for industrial transmitters in machines and is permitted for amateur radio communication only on a secondary basis.
questions.answer_d: This frequency range is used by ISM devices. Transmit powers in the amateur service must be reduced in this frequency range.

questions.question: The 80 m amateur band is allocated, among others, to the amateur service and the maritime mobile service on a primary basis. Under what circumstances may you continue an amateur contact if you notice only after starting operation that the frequency you are using is also being used by a coast station?
questions.answer_a: You may not continue to use the frequency under any circumstances (except in a genuine emergency), because the coast station has been assigned a fixed frequency that it cannot change.
questions.answer_b: You may continue to use the frequency if it is clear from the continuously repeated, automatic Morse transmission that the coast station is not carrying on two-way communication but is evidently just occupying the frequency.
questions.answer_c: You may continue to use the frequency if your amateur station is located more than 200 km from a sea coast and you are using less than 100 W of transmit power.
questions.answer_d: You may continue the contact you have started with the other station until the coast station asks you to change frequency.

questions.question: In which of the following frequency ranges does the amateur service have primary status?
How is a secondary service defined under the Amateur Radio Ordinance (Amateurfunkverordnung, AFuV)?
questions.answer_a: A secondary service is a radiocommunication service whose stations shall not cause interference to stations of a primary service and cannot claim protection from interference from such stations.
questions.answer_b: A secondary service is a radiocommunication service whose frequency assignment was made later in time. The classification does not mean that the secondary service ranks below the primary service.
questions.answer_c: A secondary service must accept interference from others and cannot report the interference to the radio interference reporting service of the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA).
questions.answer_d: The division into primary and secondary services applies only to commercial stations or to stations of authorities and organisations with security tasks.

questions.question: How is a primary service defined under the Amateur Radio Ordinance (Amateurfunkverordnung, AFuV)?
questions.answer_a: A primary service is a radiocommunication service whose stations can claim protection from interference from stations of secondary services.
questions.answer_b: Commercial stations and stations of authorities and organisations with security tasks are always stations of the primary service.
questions.answer_c: Amateur stations are not stations of a primary service, since under the provisions of the Amateur Radio Act (Amateurfunkgesetz, AFuG) amateur radio is not a safety service.
questions.answer_d: The division into primary and secondary services applies only to commercial stations or to stations of authorities and organisations with security tasks.

questions.question: Under what conditions may a radio amateur carry on radio communication in the CB band with amateur radio equipment?
questions.answer_a: A radio amateur may not transmit in the CB band with an amateur station under any circumstances.
questions.answer_b: If the radio amateur has set up the amateur radio equipment so that the technical regulations for CB radios are met
questions.answer_c: If a permit to operate CB radios is held
questions.answer_d: If the transmit power is limited to 4 W ERP for FM and AM or 12 W PEP for SSB

questions.question: Where can the frequency ranges designated for the amateur service in Germany and the associated detailed conditions of use be found?
questions.answer_a: In Annex 1 to the Amateur Radio Ordinance (Amateurfunkverordnung, AFuV) and, where applicable, further notices of the BNetzA
questions.answer_b: In Article 5 of the Radio Regulations (RR)
questions.answer_d: In the Annex to the Frequency Ordinance (FreqV)

questions.question: May a radio amateur in Germany use all the frequency ranges allocated to the amateur service in the Radio Regulations (RR)?
questions.answer_a: No, only frequencies that have been implemented by national regulations may be used.
questions.answer_b: Yes, because the international provisions of the Radio Regulations (RR) also apply in Germany.
questions.answer_c: Yes, if the operation has been registered with the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) beforehand.
questions.answer_d: No, the frequency ranges permitted in Germany follow from the Ordinance on Drawing Up the Frequency Usage Plan (Frequenznutzungsplanaufstellungsverordnung).

questions.question: Which of the following is an administrative offence under the Telecommunications Act (Telekommunikationsgesetz, TKG)?
questions.answer_a: Using frequencies without a frequency assignment
questions.answer_b: Using public telecommunications facilities to link repeaters
questions.answer_c: A radio amateur passing amateur radio messages from or to third parties
questions.answer_d: Operating an amateur station for commercial purposes

questions.question: Does every frequency use require a frequency assignment?
questions.answer_a: Every frequency use requires a prior frequency assignment.
questions.answer_b: A frequency assignment is required only from 0.1 W upwards.
questions.answer_c: There are exceptions to the need for a frequency assignment, e.g. the ISM frequencies.
questions.answer_d: Frequency use is permitted even without a frequency assignment.

questions.question: Does the Telecommunications Act (Telekommunikationsgesetz, TKG) contain provisions that apply to the amateur service?
questions.answer_a: Yes, some provisions of the TKG also apply to the amateur service.
questions.answer_b: No, for that there is the separate Amateur Radio Act (Amateurfunkgesetz, AFuG) with the Amateur Radio Ordinance (Amateurfunkverordnung, AFuV).
questions.answer_c: No, the amateur service is expressly excluded from the TKG.
questions.answer_d: Yes, all provisions of the TKG also apply to the amateur service.

sections.title: Telecommunications and Telemedia Data Protection Act (Telekommunikation-Telemedien-Datenschutz-Gesetz, TTDSG)

questions.question: For which of the following devices does the Telecommunications and Telemedia Data Protection Act (Telekommunikation-Telemedien-Datenschutz-Gesetz, TTDSG) prohibit both manufacture and possession? For ...
questions.answer_a: transmitting equipment that is disguised as another object and is therefore suitable for eavesdropping on private (non-public) conversations
questions.answer_b: scanners that allow wideband listening to the radio spectrum
questions.answer_c: directional microphones that are suitable for eavesdropping unnoticed on another person's private (non-public) conversations
questions.answer_d: digital audio players that are also suitable for making sound recordings

questions.question: What must a radio amateur do on receiving messages that are <u>not</u> intended for radio amateurs, the general public or an unspecified group of people?
questions.answer_a: Neither the content of the messages nor the fact that they were received may be communicated to others. This does not apply in emergencies and disasters.
questions.answer_b: The fact of reception may be communicated to third parties, but not the content and the details. This also applies in emergencies and disasters.
questions.answer_c: The fact of reception may be communicated to other radio amateurs, but not the content.
questions.answer_d: The receiver must be switched off immediately and the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) informed.

questions.question: By which action does a radio amateur violate the secrecy of telecommunications?
questions.answer_a: By receiving, using or passing on messages that are not intended for radio amateurs, the general public or an unspecified group of people.
questions.answer_b: By using or passing on conversation content and data from amateur radio contacts in which the radio amateur did not take part.
questions.answer_c: By using or passing on conversation content and data from amateur radio contacts, regardless of whether the radio amateur took part.
questions.answer_d: By recording and passing on conversation content and data from amateur radio contacts, in particular if they are passed on to persons who are not radio amateurs.

questions.question: May a radio amateur use the amateur station to eavesdrop on private (non-public) conversations?
questions.answer_a: Eavesdropping on private (non-public) conversations is a criminal offence.
questions.answer_b: The radio amateur counts as a competent person and may therefore decide which frequencies to listen on.
questions.answer_c: Eavesdropping on private (non-public) conversations by the radio amateur requires a special authorisation from the BNetzA.
questions.answer_d: The radio amateur is entitled to do so if technically approved receivers are used.

sections.title: Act on the Electromagnetic Compatibility of Devices (EMVG), interference cases

questions.question: Reception at your amateur station suffers recurring interference. The cause is not in your household. You want to inform the radio interference reporting service of the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA). How should you support the authority in dealing with the case?
questions.answer_a: I keep a log of the time and type of the interference and name the suspected source.
questions.answer_b: I send an e-mail every single time the interference occurs.
questions.answer_c: I press for the inspection and measurement service to be sent out quickly and phone regularly to ask about progress.
questions.answer_d: I collect the contact details of all the neighbours and report them by e-mail.

questions.question: Does a radio amateur have to accept interference to reception from other equipment?
questions.answer_a: As a rule, the interference must be accepted if the interfering equipment meets the requirements of the Act on the Electromagnetic Compatibility of Equipment (EMVG) or the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG).
questions.answer_c: The interference must be accepted in every case.
questions.answer_d: As a rule, the interference must be accepted if the interfering device is of considerable importance to its operator (e.g. an alarm system).

questions.question: Reception at your amateur station suffers interference on all bands. What should you do first?
questions.answer_a: Look for sources of interference in your own household, e.g. plug-in power supplies, LED lamps, computers and monitors.
questions.answer_b: Inform the radio interference reporting service of the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) by telephone or e-mail.
questions.answer_c: Inform the Intruder Watch of an amateur radio society.
questions.answer_d: Stop receiving immediately and switch to transmitting, for example.

questions.question: Operating an amateur station on 144.250 MHz impairs a neighbour's cable television reception. A check shows that, at the location of the affected receiving installation, the radio amateur produces a field strength below the immunity limit for cable distribution systems recommended in the standard. What does this mean for the radio amateur?
questions.answer_a: The radio amateur may continue operating.
questions.answer_b: The radio amateur must stop operating the amateur station.
questions.answer_c: The radio amateur must set the transmit power so that reception is no longer impaired.
questions.answer_d: The radio amateur may increase the transmit power without restriction.

questions.question: Operating an amateur station on 145.550 MHz impairs a neighbour's VHF broadcast receiver through direct pick-up. A check shows that, at the location of the affected receiver, the radio amateur produces a field strength below the immunity limit for equipment recommended in the standard. What does this mean for the radio amateur?
questions.answer_a: The radio amateur may continue operating.
questions.answer_b: The radio amateur must set the transmit power so that reception is no longer impaired.
questions.answer_c: The radio amateur may increase the transmit power without restriction.
questions.answer_d: The radio amateur must stop operating the amateur station.

questions.question: Operating an amateur station impairs a neighbour's television reception. A check shows that both the television set and the amateur station comply with the regulations and that no further improvements are possible. What is the BNetzA empowered to do in this case?
questions.answer_a: The BNetzA can arrange remedial measures in cooperation with those involved.
questions.answer_b: The BNetzA has no powers in this respect.
questions.answer_c: To revoke the authorisation for the amateur service immediately

questions.question: Operating an amateur station on 145.550 MHz impairs a neighbour's VHF broadcast reception. A check shows that both the amateur station and the broadcast receiving installation are operated in compliance with the regulations. What must the radio amateur expect?
questions.answer_a: Official remedial measures in cooperation with those involved
questions.answer_b: A restriction of operation subject to a fee, or a complete ban on operating the amateur station
questions.answer_c: Official measures under the AFuG, in the course of which the radio amateur's authorisation to participate in the amateur service may be withdrawn
questions.answer_d: Administrative offence proceedings with a ban on operation and a fine on the basis of the AFuG

questions.question: What is the appropriate reaction if interference to a neighbour's television or radio reception cannot be eliminated with the means available?
questions.answer_a: You politely advise the neighbour to contact the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) to have the cause of the interference examined.
questions.answer_b: The neighbour should be politely told that the cause lies in the neighbour's own installation.
questions.answer_c: The neighbour should be told that you are not responsible for this.
questions.answer_d: You notify your amateur radio society.

questions.question: Operating an amateur station interferes with a neighbour's broadcast reception. What can the radio amateur do to keep good relations with the neighbours before the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) is called in?
questions.answer_a: Reduce the transmit power for the time being.
questions.answer_b: Switch on passband tuning on the transceiver.

sections.title: Act on Making Radio Equipment Available on the Market (FuAG)

questions.question: Is proof of compliance with the technical regulations under the provisions of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG) required for radio equipment assembled by radio amateurs?
questions.answer_a: Such amateur radio equipment need not meet the requirements of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG).
questions.answer_b: Such amateur radio equipment must meet the requirements of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG).
questions.answer_c: Such amateur radio equipment is not permitted under the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG).
questions.answer_d: Such amateur radio equipment must be presented to the BNetzA for testing.

questions.question: Which regulations must commercially available receiving equipment comply with if it can receive frequencies allocated to amateur radio?
questions.answer_a: The provisions of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG) must be complied with.
questions.answer_b: In principle, amateur radio receivers do not have to comply with any provisions at all.
questions.answer_c: Essential requirements for amateur radio receivers are laid down in the Amateur Radio Ordinance (Amateurfunkverordnung, AFuV).
questions.answer_d: Amateur radio receivers may be operated only by radio amateurs; beyond that there are no further regulations.

questions.question: Which essential requirements does the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG) impose on amateur radio equipment?
questions.answer_a: Series-produced equipment must meet the essential requirements of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG) and bear the CE marking.
questions.answer_b: The radio equipment must bear a national approval marking as specified by the BNetzA.
questions.answer_c: Home-built radio equipment must meet the essential requirements of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG) and bear the CE marking.
questions.answer_d: Series-produced amateur radio equipment is not subject to the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG).

questions.question: Which equipment falls within the scope of the Radio Equipment Act (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG)?
questions.answer_a: Amateur radio equipment made available on the market
questions.answer_c: Commercially manufactured radio equipment converted for amateur radio purposes

questions.question: Which law governs, among other things, the placing on the market, the free movement and the putting into service of amateur radio equipment made available on the market?
questions.answer_c: The Act on the Electromagnetic Compatibility of Equipment (EMVG)
questions.answer_d: There are no rules for such amateur radio equipment.

sections.title: EMVU (electromagnetic compatibility with the environment) / BEMFV

questions.question: Can the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) require a site certificate for the operation of a fixed amateur station?
questions.answer_a: Only if fixed radio installations that themselves need a site certificate are already present at the location of the planned fixed amateur station.
questions.answer_b: No, the notification procedure applies to amateur radio installations
questions.answer_c: Only if the amateur station is used commercially
questions.answer_d: Yes, if the effective radiated power of the amateur station exceeds 750 W

questions.question: You want to set up an amateur station at a location where other fixed radio installations are already present. What special point must you observe regarding the protection of persons in electromagnetic fields?
questions.answer_a: If the total power of all radio installations at the location reaches or exceeds 10 W EIRP, a site certificate is required.
questions.answer_b: If the transmitter output power of the amateur station exceeds 10 W, it may not be operated at this location.
questions.answer_c: It is not permitted to operate an amateur station at a location where radio installations of other radiocommunication services are also present.
questions.answer_d: A mechanical transmit changeover switch is required that prevents the amateur radio installation from transmitting at the same time as one of the other radio installations.

questions.question: You want to operate an amateur station with several transmitting antennas and determine the safety distances for the protection of persons. It turns out that the safety distances of several antennas overlap. What must you now observe?
questions.answer_a: The antennas concerned must be considered together if they are to be used for transmitting at the same time.
questions.answer_b: The safety distance of the antenna with the highest radiated power applies to the entire antenna installation.
questions.answer_c: It must be ensured that transmission is restricted to one of the antennas at all times.
questions.answer_d: The safety distances must be multiplied by the number of transmitting antennas as a safety factor.

questions.question: Which transmissions of amateur radio installations must be taken into account when determining the site-specific safety distance?
questions.answer_a: All transmissions of the fixed amateur station that the radio amateur intends to make simultaneously
questions.answer_b: Only transmissions of amateur stations operated at a fixed location with a radiated power (EIRP) greater than 10 W
questions.answer_c: Only the transmissions at the maximum transmit power that the amateur radio installation can deliver
questions.answer_d: All transmissions with a radiated power (EIRP) greater than 10 W, including transmissions in mobile operation.

questions.question: Which procedures can radio amateurs use to produce the verification for limiting electromagnetic fields?
questions.answer_a: The assessment procedure using the "Watt Wächter" application, the simplified assessment procedure, field-strength measurement, far-field calculation and near-field calculation
questions.answer_b: Radio amateurs must commission a certified company to produce the verification for limiting electromagnetic fields.
questions.answer_c: Because of their expert knowledge, radio amateurs can estimate compliance with the electromagnetic limits.
questions.answer_d: Radio amateurs are expressly exempt from the verification for limiting electromagnetic fields.

questions.question: What must a radio amateur observe after notifying the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) of the fixed amateur station under the BEMFV?
questions.answer_a: Documentation of compliance with the requirements, with all necessary records, must be kept available, and it must be checked continuously whether the conditions under which the notification was made still apply. In the event of significant changes, the amateur station must be notified again.
questions.answer_b: By notifying the fixed amateur station, the radio amateur has fulfilled the obligations regarding the protection of persons in electromagnetic fields and need observe nothing further in this respect.
questions.answer_c: The notification procedure must be carried out again every year to keep it up to date.
questions.answer_d: Once the fixed amateur station has been put into service, the documentation of compliance with the requirements, with all necessary records, must be submitted to the competent regional office of the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA).

questions.question: In addition to the notification of a fixed amateur radio installation under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV), which documents must the radio amateur keep available from the time it is put into service and present to the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) on request?
questions.answer_a: Comprehensible documentation of compliance with the requirements, where applicable antenna patterns, a site plan, a construction drawing or sketch with dimensions, and the configuration of the radio installation
questions.answer_b: The notification form with the data of the fixed amateur radio installation and a scale sketch of the site-specific safety distance and the controllable area
questions.answer_c: The authorisation to participate in the amateur service, the data sheets of all amateur radio equipment and the log, because they must be available at all times for a possible inspection by the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA)
questions.answer_d: A photographic record of the amateur radio installation including the antennas, and an informal list of all measured values together with antenna patterns

questions.question: Which documents must be submitted to the competent regional office of the BNetzA in addition to the notification of a fixed amateur radio installation under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV)?
questions.answer_a: A comprehensible drawing of the site-specific safety distance and of the area controllable by the operator must be attached to the notification.
questions.answer_b: Antenna patterns, a site plan, a construction drawing or sketch with dimensions must be attached to the notification.
questions.answer_c: No further documents need to be attached.
questions.answer_d: A block diagram of the amateur station must be attached.

questions.question: What status does the notification of a fixed amateur radio installation have in the context of EMVU?
questions.answer_a: The notification is the radio amateur's binding declaration that the statutory limits for the protection of persons in electromagnetic fields are complied with on the radio amateur's own responsibility.
questions.answer_b: The notification is a non-binding declaration that radio amateurs act on their own responsibility.
questions.answer_c: The notification has the same legal status as a site certificate, but applies only to non-commercial installations.
questions.answer_d: The notification is the radio amateur's binding declaration that the Federal Immission Control Act (BImSchG) is complied with on the radio amateur's own responsibility.

questions.question: When must a notification of a fixed amateur radio installation under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV) be submitted again to the competent office of the BNetzA?
questions.answer_a: If the existing notification no longer corresponds to the actual circumstances, the operator must carry out the notification procedure again.
questions.answer_b: The notification must be updated every year. If no changes have been made to the amateur radio installation, an informal message is sufficient.
questions.answer_c: When the national certificate class changes
questions.answer_d: When requested by the competent office of the BNetzA

questions.question: To which office and at what time must the notification under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV) be submitted for a fixed amateur radio installation with an EIRP of 10 W or more?
questions.answer_a: The notification must be submitted to the competent regional office of the BNetzA before the amateur radio installation is put into operation.
questions.answer_b: The notification must be submitted to the competent regional office of the BNetzA no later than three months after operation has started.
questions.answer_c: If the notification no longer corresponds to the actual circumstances, any regional office of the BNetzA must be informed of this.
questions.answer_d: The notification must be submitted to any regional office of the BNetzA before the amateur radio installation is put into operation.

questions.question: Who must notify the BNetzA of their amateur station under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV)?
questions.answer_a: All radio amateurs who operate fixed amateur stations with a power of 10 W EIRP or more
questions.answer_b: All radio amateurs who operate portable or mobile
questions.answer_c: All radio amateurs of certificate class A
questions.answer_d: All radio amateurs who are active on HF

questions.question: For which amateur stations must the radio amateur document the protection of persons in electromagnetic fields?
questions.answer_a: For all fixed amateur stations with an equivalent isotropically radiated power of 10 W EIRP or more
questions.answer_d: For all amateur stations with an equivalent isotropically radiated power of 10 W EIRP or more

questions.question: What must a radio amateur do to protect persons when operating fixed amateur radio installations under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV)?
questions.answer_a: The safety distance required to comply with the limits must be determined by calculation or measurement for a radio installation with an EIRP of 10 W or more and documented in a comprehensible form.
questions.answer_b: Up to a power of 100 W PEP, the standardised safety distance of 10 m can be assumed.
questions.answer_c: Up to a power of 100 W PEP, the standardised safety distance of 25 m can be assumed.
questions.answer_d: The safety distance required to comply with the limits must be determined by a certified measurement laboratory.

questions.question: Where are the limits for the protection of persons and active implants in electromagnetic fields laid down?
questions.answer_a: In the 26th Ordinance implementing the Federal Immission Control Act (Ordinance on Electromagnetic Fields, 26. BImSchV) and in the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV)
questions.answer_b: In the Directive on the electromagnetic compatibility of electrical and electronic products (EMC Directive) and in the Act on the Electromagnetic Compatibility of Equipment (EMVG)
questions.answer_c: In the Act on Making Radio Equipment Available on the Market (Funkanlagengesetz, FuAG) and in the Telecommunications Act (Telekommunikationsgesetz, TKG)
questions.answer_d: In the Act on Amateur Radio (Amateurfunkgesetz, AFuG) and in the Ordinance under the Act on Amateur Radio (Amateurfunkverordnung, AFuV)

questions.question: Under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV), what is meant by the "notification procedure for fixed amateur radio installations"?
questions.answer_a: A procedure that enables radio amateurs to ensure and document independently that there is no danger to persons
questions.answer_b: A procedure that a certified measurement laboratory must carry out to ensure that there is no danger to persons
questions.answer_c: The radio amateur's declaration that the power stays below the limit of 10 W EIRP
questions.answer_d: The radio amateur's declaration that the power does not exceed the limit of 750 W PEP

questions.question: In which statutory provision is the procedure for the protection of persons in electromagnetic fields of fixed amateur stations laid down?
questions.answer_a: In the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV)
questions.answer_b: In the Amateur Radio Act (Amateurfunkgesetz, AFuG)
questions.answer_d: In the Federal Immission Control Act (BImSchG)

questions.question: Who is responsible for ensuring electromagnetic compatibility with the environment?
questions.answer_a: The operator of the fixed amateur station
questions.answer_c: The manufacturer of the amateur radio equipment
questions.answer_d: The builder of the antenna installation

questions.question: What does the abbreviation EMVU stand for?
questions.answer_a: Electromagnetic compatibility with the environment (Elektromagnetische Verträglichkeit in der Umwelt)
questions.answer_b: Electromagnetic compatibility of devices (Elektromagnetische Verträglichkeit von Geräten)
questions.answer_c: Electronic measurement of electromagnetic incompatibilities (Elektronische Messung von elektromagnetischen Unverträglichkeiten)
questions.answer_d: A citizens' initiative for protection against electromagnetic incompatibilities

questions.question: Under what conditions must standard VDE 0855-300 for equipotential bonding and earthing of radio installations, and the series of standards VDE 0185-305 for lightning protection, be applied?
questions.answer_a: Standard VDE 0855-300 applies to all amateur radio transmitting installations. The series of standards VDE 0185-305 applies only to buildings with a lightning protection system.
questions.answer_b: Both standards must be applied when buildings can be struck by lightning.
questions.answer_c: If the antenna installation is far enough away from the building, the series of standards VDE 0185-305 need not be applied.
questions.answer_d: Standard VDE 0855-300 applies to buildings on which antennas are erected. Wire antennas and free-standing antenna masts are exempt from it.

questions.question: In which set of rules are recognised codes of practice for the lightning protection of amateur antenna installations to be found?
questions.answer_b: Provisions of the Amateur Radio Act (Amateurfunkgesetz, AFuG)
questions.answer_c: Lightning protection regulations of the competent building control authority
questions.answer_d: Rules of the amateur radio societies

questions.question: Under which building regulations must outdoor antenna installations be erected?
questions.answer_a: The building regulations of the relevant federal state apply.
questions.answer_b: The provisions of the Amateur Radio Act (Amateurfunkgesetz, AFuG) apply.
questions.answer_c: Only the recommendations of the amateur radio societies need to be observed.
questions.answer_d: No special regulations need to be observed for private amateur radio installations.

questions.question: How must the power supply of home-built equipment be constructed to be electrically safe?
questions.answer_a: In accordance with the recognised codes of practice, as laid down for example in the VDE standards.
questions.answer_b: No special regulations apply, since a radio amateur is a competent person.
questions.answer_c: The regulations of the local electricity supplier apply.
questions.answer_d: It must be constructed in accordance with the CEPT recommendations.

questions.question: Who is liable for damage to third parties that may be caused by the antenna installation of an amateur station?
questions.answer_a: The owner or operator of the antenna installation
questions.answer_b: The amateur radio society, if the operator of the amateur station is a member of such a society
questions.answer_c: The Federal Network Agency (BNetzA), since the monthly contributions include a share for group insurance for radio amateurs' antenna installations.
questions.answer_d: The owner of the property, who must take out antenna liability insurance even if not the operator of the amateur station.

questions.question: May an amateur station also be operated on board a ship that is in international waters?
questions.answer_a: Yes, with the consent of the master
questions.answer_b: Yes, with the consent of any crew member
questions.answer_c: Yes, with a permit from the BNetzA
questions.answer_d: Yes, with a permit from the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency

questions.question: What requirement must be met for you to be allowed to operate amateur radio on board an aircraft?
questions.answer_a: Consent of the pilot in command
questions.answer_b: Permission from the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) for aeronautical radio operation
questions.answer_c: Use of a permanently installed station of the aeronautical mobile service
questions.answer_d: Use of frequencies allocated to the aeronautical mobile service

questions.question: What consequences must the radio amateur expect if the fees and contributions due are not paid?
questions.answer_a: Measures under the provisions of the Administrative Enforcement Act.
questions.answer_b: Withdrawal of the amateur radio certificate.
questions.answer_d: A re-examination subject to a fee.

questions.question: In which case must the radio amateur pay fees under the Special Fees Ordinance of the BNetzA (BNetzABGebV)? For the ...
questions.answer_a: issue of the authorisation to participate in the amateur service and assignment of a personal call sign.
questions.answer_b: examination of the documents to be submitted under the Ordinance on the Verification Procedure for Limiting Electromagnetic Fields (BEMFV).
questions.answer_c: testing of the electromagnetic compatibility of an amateur station.
questions.answer_d: short-term relocation of the fixed amateur station to another location.

questions.question: In which case must the radio amateur pay annual contributions under the Frequency Protection Contribution Ordinance (FSBeitrV)? Whenever the radio amateur ...
questions.answer_a: holds an authorisation for the amateur service.
questions.answer_c: owns and has set up an amateur station.
questions.answer_d: owns, has set up and operates an amateur station.

questions.question: Which regular contributions does a radio amateur with a call sign assignment have to pay?
questions.answer_a: Annual frequency protection contributions under the TKG and the EMVG
questions.answer_b: Annual assignment contributions under the provisions of the AFuG
questions.answer_c: No contributions if the radio amateur is a member of an amateur radio society
questions.answer_d: No contributions if the radio amateur has a call sign assignment but has not set up or does not operate an amateur station
